text: That man is free, who lives as he wishes, who is proof against compulsion and hindrance and violence, whose impulses are untrammelled, who gets what he wills to get and avoids what he wills to avoid.
plain: You are free when nothing can force you off your own path.

text: The softer he lives, the worse is his slavery.
plain: The more comfort you need, the more things own you.

text: Keep your hands far away from it; above all, keep your will away, or else you surrender yourself into slavery, you put your neck under the yoke, if you admire what is not your own, and set your heart on anything mortal, whatever it be, or anything that depends upon another.
plain: Whatever you cling to that someone else can take, you have handed them control of you.

text: How then is the citadel destroyed? Not by fire or sword, but by judgements.
plain: The fight that matters is inside your head, not out there.

text: You have received everything, nay your very self, from Another, and yet you complain and blame the Giver, if He takes anything away from you.
plain: You were lent all of it. Complaining when it goes back is ungrateful.

text: Purify your judgements, and see that nothing that is not your own is attached to you or clings to you, that nothing shall give you pain if it is torn from you.
plain: Hold nothing so tight that losing it would wreck you.

text: No one can do wrong acts with impunity.
plain: Doing wrong always costs the one who does it.

text: For freedom is secured not by the fulfilling of men's desires, but by the removal of desire.
plain: You get free by wanting less, not by getting more.

text: When you do not drink with those whom you used to drink with, you cannot seem as agreeable to them as of old; choose then, whether you wish to be a drinker and gratify them, or sober and displease them.
plain: Changing means some people will like you less. Pick which you want.

text: If you give up any external possession, mind you see what you are to get in exchange for it: and if it is worth more, then never say, 'I have been a loser.'
plain: Giving something up is a trade. If you get something better, you lost nothing.

text: Regard for any external thing, whatever it be, makes you subservient to another.
plain: Whatever you need from the outside gives someone else a hold on you.

text: If reading does not win you peace of mind, what is the good of it?
plain: Learning that doesn't change how you live is wasted.

text: To ask for books is as though an athlete should complain, as he enters the arena, that he is not training outside.
plain: Stop preparing. The game has started.

text: Life is what you were training for all along, this is what the leaping-weights, and the sawdust, and the young men you wrestled with were leading up to.
plain: All the practice was for this. Now do it.

text: How long are you going to exercise yourself in solitude? The time has now come for you to discover whether you are an athlete worthy of victory, or one of those who go about the world suffering continual defeat.
plain: Practice is over. Time to find out what you are made of.

text: There is no conflict without a crowd: there must be many to train beforehand, many to cry applause, many stewards, many spectators.
plain: Hard tests come with an audience. That is part of the setup.

text: You do not call a man industrious who keeps late hours for the sake of a mistress: neither do I. But if he does it for glory, I call him ambitious; if for money, I call him fond of money, not fond of work.
plain: Ask what you are really chasing when you grind.

text: You are no piece of crockery: you are a rational will.
plain: What breaks around you is not you.

text: What do you care for them? No craftsman cares for those who have no skill!
plain: Don't take opinions from people who can't judge the work.

text: Do we not remember that one man does not harm nor benefit another? It is man's judgement on each situation that harms him.
plain: What hurts you is how you read what happened.

text: What is that to me, if I make up my mind that it is nothing to me?
plain: An insult only lands if you agree it matters.

text: In the lecture-room we are lions, and foxes in the world outside!
plain: Everyone is brave in theory. Live it when it counts.

text: It is the part of a king, Cyrus, to do well and be ill-spoken of.
plain: Doing right and getting slandered for it comes with the job.

text: Some one flings a shower of figs and nuts: the children try to seize them, and fight with one another for them; grown men do not, for they count it a small matter.
plain: Titles and status are scraps. Grown people don't scramble for them.

text: Well! does the Emperor himself, and you who obey him, keep his neck for ever?
plain: The powerful die too. Nobody holds on forever.

text: 'Would you give me poverty?' Give it me and you shall learn what poverty is when a good actor plays the part.
plain: Poverty only crushes you if you play the part badly.

text: Do not use fine words, but state the facts as they are.
plain: Skip the fancy words and say plainly what is there.

text: Only try your authority and you will learn how far it extends.
plain: Their power stops at your body and your stuff. Your mind is out of reach.

text: Seeing then that I neither fear anything that he can do to me nor desire anything that he can provide, why do I stand in awe and amazement before him any more?
plain: Want nothing from someone and fear nothing from them, and they have no power over you.

text: So long as you busy yourself with external things, no one will succeed with them so well as you, but this faculty of reason will be, what your own choice makes it, mouldy and neglected.
plain: You can be great at the outside game and let your own mind rot.

text: Study first not to let men know what you are: keep your philosophy to yourself for a little.
plain: Build quietly before you announce anything.

text: The seed must needs be buried first, and be hidden, and increase by slow degrees, that it may come to fullness.
plain: Growth starts out of sight and takes its time.

text: That is the sort of plant you are: you have blossomed sooner than you ought, and will wither away when the storm comes.
plain: Showing off before you have roots means the first hard season takes you out.

text: See how I eat, how I drink, how I sleep, how I bear and forbear, how I work for others, how I exercise the will to get and the will to avoid, how I observe my relationships, natural and acquired, without confusion and without hindrance. Judge me by this, if you can.
plain: Judge a person by how they live every day, not by how they look.

text: Was it by proclaiming aloud, 'This is the man I am'? Never! but by being the man he was.
plain: Be it. Don't announce it.

text: When you see another man in office, set against his office the fact that you have no need of office: when you see another rich, look what you have instead.
plain: Against their wealth and rank, count what you don't need.

text: Fight against yourself, deliver yourself, that you may be modest, self-respecting, free.
plain: The enemy is you. Beat that one.

text: The boy has fallen, suppose. 'Get up', says the trainer, 'and wrestle again, until you are made strong.'
plain: You fell. Get up and go again.

text: You have but to will a thing and it is done, and all is right; on the other hand you have but to relax your effort and all is lost. For destruction and deliverance lie within you.
plain: Your effort decides whether you rise or fall.

text: All men's difficulties and perplexities are concerned with external things.
plain: Most of your worry is about stuff you don't control.

text: Say no more then, 'What is to happen?' For whatever happens, you will turn it to good purpose, and the issue will be your good fortune.
plain: Stop asking what will happen. Decide how you'll use whatever does.

text: What care you, I say? If a big boar appears, you will have a greater struggle to engage in; if evil men appear, you will free the world from evil men.
plain: A bigger enemy just means a bigger fight to win.

text: What then would you have death find you doing?
plain: Live so that whenever it ends, you were doing something worth doing.

text: No, if you wish for what is not your own, you lose what is yours. This is in the nature of things: nothing is done but at a price.
plain: Chasing what isn't yours costs you what is. Everything has a price.

text: Will you not weigh what the exchange is and how precious your gain, instead of wishing to obtain this great prize for nothing?
plain: Nothing big comes free. Decide if the price is worth it.

text: You cannot combine attention to outward possessions with attention to your own Governing Principle.
plain: You can't chase stuff and master yourself at the same time.

text: When you relax your attention for a little, do not imagine that you will recover it wherever you wish, but bear this well in mind, that your error of to-day must of necessity put you in a worse position for other occasions.
plain: Every lapse makes the next one easier. You don't get to pick up focus on demand.

text: Do you not realize, that when once you have let your mind go wandering, you lose the power to recall it, to bring it to bear on what is seemly, self-respecting, and modest: you do anything that occurs to you and follow your inclinations?
plain: Let your attention drift and you end up doing whatever comes to mind.

text: What then? Is it possible to escape error altogether? No, it is impossible: but it is possible to set one's mind continuously on avoiding error.
plain: You won't be perfect. Keep aiming at fewer mistakes anyway.

text: As it is, you say, 'I will fix my attention to-morrow': which means, let me tell you, 'To-day I will be shameless, inopportune, abject: others shall have power to vex me: to-day I will harbour anger and envy.'
plain: Saying you'll start tomorrow means you choose to be weak today.

text: That is just as though I had a sound cask and you an unsound one, and you came and handed over your wine to me to put it into my cask, and then were vexed that I did not trust my wine to you, because your cask had a hole in it.
plain: Someone who spills everything to everyone hasn't earned your secrets.

text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
plain: Sort everything into what you control and what you don't. Work only on the first.

text: Straightway then practise saying to every harsh appearance: You are an appearance, and in no manner what you appear to be.
plain: When something looks terrible, tell yourself it's just how it looks right now.

text: But if you attempt to avoid disease, or death, or poverty, you will be unhappy.
plain: You can't dodge sickness, death, or lack. Trying to just makes you miserable.

text: If you love an earthen vessel, say it is an earthen vessel which you love; for when it has been broken you will not be disturbed.
plain: Remember what a thing is, and losing it won't wreck you.

text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing.
plain: It's not events that hurt you, it's the story you tell about them.

text: When then we are impeded, or disturbed, or grieved, let us never blame others, but ourselves—that is, our opinions.
plain: When you're upset, look at your own thinking first.

text: It is the act of an ill-instructed man to blame others for his own bad condition; it is the act of one who has begun to be instructed, to lay the blame on himself; and of one whose instruction is completed, neither to blame another, nor himself.
plain: Beginners blame others, learners blame themselves, masters just deal with it.

text: What then is your own? The use of appearances.
plain: What you really own is how you respond to what comes at you.

text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
plain: Stop demanding that things go your way. Want what happens and you stay calm.

text: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses. Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will.
plain: Your body can be blocked. Your will only stops if you let it.

text: On the occasion of every accident (event) that befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use.
plain: When something hits you, ask what you can do with it.

text: If labor (pain) be presented to you, you will find that it is endurance. If it be abusive words, you will find it to be patience.
plain: Every hardship hands you the exact strength it takes to meet it.

text: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.
plain: Nothing was ever yours to keep. Say it went back, not that you lost it.

text: Is the oil spilled? Is a little wine stolen? Say on the occasion, at such price is sold freedom from perturbation; at such price is sold tranquillity, but nothing is got for nothing.
plain: Small losses are the price of staying calm, and it's cheap.

text: If you would improve, submit to be considered without sense and foolish with respect to externals.
plain: Growing means being willing to look clueless to people who don't matter.

text: Wish to be considered to know nothing; and if you shall seem to some to be a person of importance, distrust yourself.
plain: When people start treating you as important, get suspicious of yourself.

text: But if you wish not to fail in your desires, you are able to do that.
plain: You can never fail at your desires if you only want what is within your reach.

text: Whoever then wishes to be free let him neither wish for anything nor avoid anything which depends on others: if he does not observe this rule, he must be a slave.
plain: If your wants depend on other people, they own you.

text: Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet. Suppose that something is carried round and is opposite to you. Stretch out your hand and take a portion with decency.
plain: When good things come around, take your share politely. Don't grab or chase.

text: For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.
plain: You don't pick your role. You pick how well you play it.

text: You can be invincible, if you enter into no contest in which it is not in your power to conquer.
plain: Only fight the battles you can actually win, and you can't lose.

text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting.
plain: An insult hurts only because you decide it does.

text: Let death and exile and every other thing which appears dreadful be daily before your eyes; but most of all death: and you will never think of anything mean nor will you desire anything extravagantly.
plain: Keep death in view and petty wants shrink.

text: If I can acquire money and also keep myself modest and faithful and magnanimous, point out the way, and I will acquire it.
plain: Money is fine if getting it doesn't cost me my character.

text: You will be unjust then and insatiable, if you do not part with the price, in return for which those things are sold, and if you wish to obtain them for nothing.
plain: Don't expect what others got without paying what they paid.

text: If any person was intending to put your body in the power of any man whom you fell in with on the way, you would be vexed; but that you put your understanding in the power of any man whom you meet, so that if he should revile you, it is disturbed and troubled, are you not ashamed at this?
plain: You'd never hand a stranger your body, so why hand over your mood?

text: A man wishes to conquer at the Olympic games. I also wish indeed, for it is a fine thing. But observe both the things which come first, and the things which follow; and then begin the act.
plain: Everyone wants the win. Look at what it demands before you sign up.

text: So you also will be at one time an athlete, at another a gladiator, then a rhetorician, then a philosopher, but with your whole soul you will be nothing at all; but like an ape you imitate everything that you see, and one thing after another pleases you.
plain: Hopping between ideas of who you could be leaves you nobody.

text: You must pass sleepless nights, endure toil, go away from your kinsmen, be despised by a slave, in everything have the inferior part, in honor, in office, in the courts of justice, in every little matter.
plain: The path costs sleep, comfort, home, and respect. Know it going in.

text: You must be one man, either good or bad.
plain: Pick who you are and be that all the way.

text: Immediately prescribe some character and some form to yourself, which you shall observe both when you are alone and when you meet with men.
plain: Decide who you are and act that way alone and in public.

text: And let silence be the general rule, or let only what is necessary be said, and in few words.
plain: Talk less. Say what's needed.

text: If a man has reported to you, that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make any defence (answer) to what has been told you; but reply, The man did not know the rest of my faults, for he would not have mentioned these only.
plain: When someone trashes you, don't defend yourself. Joke that they didn't know the half of it.

text: In company take care not to speak much and excessively about your own acts or dangers; for as it is pleasant to you to make mention of your own dangers, it is not so pleasant to others to hear what has happened to you.
plain: Your stories thrill you and bore everyone else.

text: If you have received the impression of any pleasure, guard yourself against being carried away by it; but let the thing wait for you, and allow yourself a certain delay on your own part.
plain: Feel the urge, then make it wait.

text: Then think of both times, of the time when you will enjoy the pleasure, and of the time after the enjoyment of the pleasure, when you will repent and will reproach yourself.
plain: Picture the pleasure, then picture the regret after it.

text: When you have decided that a thing ought to be done, and are doing it, never avoid being seen doing it, though the many shall form an unfavorable opinion about it. For if it is not right to do it, avoid doing the thing; but if it is right, why are you afraid of those who shall find fault wrongly?
plain: If it's right, do it in public and ignore the critics.

text: The measure of possession (property) is to every man the body, as the foot is of the shoe.
plain: Own what you need. Past that there's no natural stopping point.

text: When any person treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember that he does this or says this because he thinks that it is his duty.
plain: People who treat you badly think they're in the right.

text: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not.
plain: Every situation has a part you can carry. Grab that one.

text: On no occasion call yourself a philosopher, and do not speak much among the uninstructed about theorems (philosophical rules, precepts); but do that which follows from them.
plain: Don't preach your principles. Live them.

text: And when a man shall say to you that you know nothing, and you are not vexed, then be sure that you have begun the work (of philosophy).
plain: If being called clueless no longer stings, you're getting somewhere.

text: For even sheep do not vomit up their grass and show to the shepherds how much they have eaten; but when they have internally digested the pasture, they produce externally wool and milk.
plain: Don't show off what you've read. Let it turn into results.

text: And if you ever wish to exercise yourself in labor and endurance, do it for yourself, and not for others.
plain: Train hard for yourself, not for an audience.

text: Do not embrace statues; but if you are ever very thirsty, take a draught of cold water and spit it out, and tell no man.
plain: Practice hardship privately and keep quiet about it.

text: The condition and characteristic of an uninstructed person is this: he never expects from himself profit (advantage) nor harm, but from externals. The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is this: he expects all advantage and all harm from himself.
plain: Weak people wait for luck or blame the world. Strong people look at themselves.

text: When, then, any man says to me, Read Chrysippus to me, I rather blush, when I cannot show my acts like to and consistent with his words.
plain: Knowing the ideas means little if your actions don't match.

text: How long will you then still defer thinking yourself worthy of the best things, and in no matter transgressing the distinctive reason?
plain: How long will you wait before you hold yourself to a higher standard?

text: You are no longer a youth, but already a full-grown man.
plain: You're not a kid anymore. Act like it now.

text: And if anything laborious or pleasant or glorious or inglorious be presented to you, remember that now is the contest, now are the Olympic games, and they cannot be deferred; and that it depends on one defeat and one giving way that progress is either lost or maintained.
plain: This moment is the real test, and one slip decides whether you keep your progress.

text: But you, though you are not yet a Socrates, ought to live as one who wishes to be a Socrates.
plain: You're not there yet. Live like someone who is trying to be.

text: Lead me, O Zeus, and thou O Destiny, The way that I am bid by you to go: To follow I am ready. If I choose not, I make myself a wretch, and still must follow.
plain: Fate moves either way. Go willingly or get dragged.

text: O Crito, if so it pleases the gods, so let it be; Anytus and Melitus are able indeed to kill me, but they cannot harm me.
plain: They can take my life, but not my character.
